lead.headline: Notices to vacate fall due today on nine shops in the Vantry Arcade
lead.deck: No agent of Signal Ground Rents Inc. had called by 9 p.m.; the tenants to open at the usual hours; Mr. Bliss's luncheonette stayed to May 27
lead.body: Notices to vacate served by Signal Ground Rents Inc. on nine tenants of the Vantry Arcade fall due today, the tenants state. No agent of the company had called at the Arcade by 9 p.m. yesterday, and no locks had been changed. All nine tenants stated that they will open at the usual hours. Mr. Oscar Bliss's luncheonette, the tenth shop served, is stayed by order of Judge Peter Hanrahan until May 27. The company's post office box at Long Island City remains 'not rented.'

columns.headline: May Day march permitted from Queensboro Plaza to Astoria Park at 2 p.m.
columns.body: The Police Department has granted the United Workers' Committee of Queens a permit to march from Queensboro Plaza to Astoria Park at 2 p.m. today. Captain Thomas Galvin states that the Department's sound wagon will record the speeches. The Committee states that it will record them also.

columns.headline: Light rate of 7.5 cents and ice at 45 cents in effect from today
columns.body: Queens Light & Power's domestic rate of 7.5 cents the kilowatt-hour and the ice companies' price of 45 cents the hundredweight take effect today. The Astoria Lake Ice Co. states that its Steinway wagon will be drawn by Duchess, a bay mare aged seven, in place of Major.

columns.headline: Mr. Crane grants 52 licences under the Act; 274 granted in all
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane, Deputy Secretary of State, heard 60 applicants under the Listening Act at the Borough Hall yesterday and granted 52 licences, 274 in all. Of 6,000 forms delivered on April 9, 1,388 have been returned. Licences are required from July 1.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the twentieth night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 61. Wednesday. May Day. The Reds march, and the police bring a machine.

lead.headline: May Day speeches go on the record twice, and the police get the B side
lead.deck: Three thousand march from Queensboro Plaza behind a brass band; the sound wagon takes down six speakers, and the Committee's own machine takes down the sound wagon
lead.body: At two this afternoon about three thousand men and women of the United Workers' Committee marched from Queensboro Plaza to Astoria Park behind a brass band that knew two tunes and played both. Six speakers stood on a coal cart. The Police Department's sound wagon was parked on the left of the cart, recording every word, and the Committee's own machine was parked on the right, recording every word and the sound wagon. Captain Galvin was polite. The speeches were long. Nobody threw anything but a hat.

columns.headline: Nine Arcade shops stay open on notice, and the landlord never rings the bell
columns.body: The notices fell due this morning and the nine shops opened at the usual hours. Alderman Feeney and Duke stood at the entrance from nine. Nobody came. Nobody came at noon. Then at twenty to four a man in a grey coat walked in off the street. More tomorrow.

columns.headline: Duchess takes the Steinway route, and makes some unscheduled connections
columns.body: The ice company's new horse, Duchess, aged seven, took the Steinway wagon out at six this morning at the new price of forty-five cents. She does not know the route. She stopped at a barber's, a church and a dentist's. The kitchens are being patient. Major would never.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Twenty nights of dead air, and the Speaker keeps ringing
columns.body: Having rung the Radio Division yesterday, this newspaper now rings it every night at eleven, when WORS used to come on. Mr. Pike's night clerk has begun to say 'No' before we ask. It is the most reliable service in Queens.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Light is seven and a half cents from midnight. This edition was written by the window.

lead.headline: May Day march of 3,100 to Astoria Park; six speeches taken down by two machines
lead.deck: The Police Department's sound wagon and the United Workers' Committee's machine set either side of the speakers' cart; Mr. Karl Ostrow arrested at 4:52 p.m. 'on the Department's record'
lead.body: About 3,100 persons marched from Queensboro Plaza to Astoria Park yesterday under a permit to the United Workers' Committee of Queens. Six speeches were made from a coal cart between 3:05 p.m. and 4:40 p.m. and were recorded by the Department's sound wagon and by the Committee's own machine. Mr. Karl Ostrow, a tinsmith of Astoria, the fifth speaker, was arrested at 4:52 p.m. and charged with incitement 'on the Department's record.' The Committee states that its record 'says otherwise.'

columns.headline: Nine Arcade tenants state the May rent was collected in cash at 3:40 p.m.
columns.body: Nine tenants of the Vantry Arcade state that a man in a grey coat called at each shop between 3:40 p.m. and 4:15 p.m. yesterday and collected the May rent in cash, giving receipts initialled 'S.G.R.' He gave no name.

columns.headline: Berlin police and May Day marchers clash in Wedding and Neukolln
columns.body: The Berlin wire reports that police and May Day marchers fought in the Wedding and Neukolln districts yesterday in defiance of a ban on demonstrations, and that several persons were killed. The fighting was heard at the wire office 'until after midnight.'

columns.headline: Mr. Crane grants 55 licences; first form received from a house of worship
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 55 licences under the Listening Act at the Borough Hall yesterday, 329 in all. His office states that it has received its first form from a house of worship, returned unsigned, 'with a letter.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Karl Ostrow was released on 500 dollars' bail at 9:40 p.m. and will appear before Magistrate Leonard Haber at 10 a.m. tomorrow.

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 58. Thursday. Rent day came in a grey coat.

lead.headline: Grey coat collects the Arcade's rent, and leaves no number to call back
lead.deck: The landlord who never answers sends a man who never says his name; nine shops on notice pay May's rent anyway and get receipts signed S.G.R.; Duke growls once
lead.body: At twenty to four yesterday, with Alderman Feeney gone home and the nine shops open on their notices, a man in a grey coat came into the Vantry Arcade from the street, went to each counter and said 'May.' Each tenant paid him in cash, not quite knowing why. He wrote receipts initialled S.G.R. in a good clerk's hand. He gave no name. Duke, who had stayed, growled once. At a quarter past four the man walked out the way he came, and nobody followed him.

columns.headline: Two machines take down May Day, and the copper's copy plays a different tune
columns.body: Six speakers on a coal cart in Astoria Park, a machine on either side. Mr. Ostrow, tinsmith, was arrested at eight minutes to five on the police record. The Committee says its own record has him saying something else. Tomorrow a magistrate gets to listen to both.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Does a church need a licence to hear a prayer?'
columns.body: Sir, Mr. Crane has received his first licence form from a church, unsigned, with a letter. We have not seen the letter. The operator has views. She says the question is who signs for the building, and that the answer is above her board.

columns.headline: Dolan puts his ear to a manhole, and Steinway Street listens back
columns.body: Mr. Dolan, who would open a borough office to hear the ground, spent May Day afternoon kneeling at a manhole on Steinway Street before a crowd of forty. He says he heard the subway. There is no subway under Steinway Street. He says that is his point.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Ostrow is out on five hundred dollars. He says the police machine wants its ears syringed.

lead.headline: Counsel for Mr. Bliss asks whether rent paid on May 1 waives the nine notices
lead.deck: Mr. Nathan Ewald cites the receipts initialled 'S.G.R.'; the collector described by six tenants as 'about fifty, grey coat, no hat'; the Arcade's own system took down his visit
lead.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald, counsel for Mr. Oscar Bliss, stated yesterday that the acceptance of the May rent by an agent of Signal Ground Rents Inc. on May 1 'may waive the notices to vacate' served on nine other tenants of the Vantry Arcade, and that he will put the receipts before Judge Peter Hanrahan on May 27. Six tenants describe the collector as 'about fifty, grey coat, no hat, a clerk's hand.' The Arcade's house system recorded his footsteps and the word 'May,' nine times.

columns.headline: Brooklyn Exchange logs 212 night calls on a tone in Greenpoint and Williamsburg
columns.body: The Brooklyn Exchange logged 212 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. on Tuesday and Wednesday nights from subscribers in Greenpoint and Williamsburg reporting 'a low tone,' its superintendent, Mr. Oswald Pryce, states. It is the first such count from Brooklyn.

columns.headline: Magistrate Haber to hear both records of Mr. Ostrow's speech at 10 a.m. today
columns.body: Magistrate Leonard Haber has subpoenaed the Police Department's record and the United Workers' Committee's record of Mr. Karl Ostrow's speech in Astoria Park on May 1, and will hear both at 10 a.m. today in the Long Island City Magistrate's Court.

columns.headline: Detective Sergeant Moran states the warrant for Mr. Marchetti 'is current'
columns.body: Detective Sergeant Edward Moran states that the warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, 'is current and is being served as occasion allows.' No purchaser of the Portland sardine has been reported at the Corona grocer's since the watch was discontinued.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Brooklyn Courier states that 'no tone has been heard in Brooklyn and none is expected.'

speaker.ear: Fair. High 64. Friday. Brooklyn has the Hum. Brooklyn says it doesn't.

lead.headline: The Hum crosses Newtown Creek, and Brooklyn says it's a wrong number
lead.deck: Two hundred and twelve Greenpoint and Williamsburg callers report a low tone at night; the Brooklyn Courier says nobody heard anything and nobody will; Queens offers sympathy and a meter
lead.body: The Hum has been a Queens complaint, like the ash dumps. This week two hundred and twelve people in Greenpoint and Williamsburg rang the Brooklyn Exchange between one and four in the morning to report a low tone. The Brooklyn Courier, which has always thought Queens hears things, says flatly that no tone has been heard in Brooklyn and none is expected. Two hundred and twelve Brooklynites have been told they did not hear what they heard. Queens knows the feeling. Dr. Rastin is available.

columns.headline: Party Line holds the four o'clock again, and the line stays dead
columns.body: Five Fridays. Party Line took her place in the parcel window at four with her tail round her feet. Sergeant Moran says the lineman's warrant is current and served as occasion allows. No occasion allowed. At six she went to the warm end of the board and slept.

columns.headline: Grey coat says 'May' nine times, and the Arcade's walls take the minutes
columns.body: The Arcade's own system recorded the rent man's footsteps and one word, May, nine times. Mr. Ewald, Mr. Bliss's lawyer, says taking the rent may cancel the notices. So the man who came to collect may have come to forgive. He did not look the type.

columns.headline: Ostrow faces the music in two keys, and the records part company at the mills
columns.body: Magistrate Haber played both records of Mr. Ostrow's speech this morning. They agree for eleven minutes. Then the police have him taking the mills, and the Committee has him taking the mills to the courts. Three words. Neither machine skipped. Thursday, says the magistrate.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Courier's night editor rang ours at two this morning to say there was no tone. Ours could hear it behind him.

lead.headline: Two records of Mr. Ostrow's May Day speech differ by three words, court finds
lead.deck: Played together in the Long Island City court at 10:15 a.m.; the police record 'we will take the mills'; the Committee's 'we will take the mills to the courts'; decision reserved to Thursday
lead.body: Magistrate Leonard Haber heard the Police Department's record and the United Workers' Committee's record of Mr. Karl Ostrow's speech of May 1 played together in the Long Island City Magistrate's Court at 10:15 a.m. yesterday. They agree for 11 minutes and differ at 4:31 p.m. by three words. The police record has Mr. Ostrow: 'and then we will take the mills.' The Committee's has: 'and then we will take the mills to the courts.' Neither shows a break. Decision is reserved.

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,240 night calls on the tone in Queens; 212 in Brooklyn
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,240 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 1,186 the week before, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The Brooklyn Exchange logged 212. Dr. Emil Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles.

columns.headline: Brooklyn Courier's editor states the 212 callers 'have relatives in Queens'
columns.body: Mr. Ambrose Tully, editor of the Brooklyn Courier, states in a signed notice that 'no tone has been heard in Brooklyn,' and that the 212 calls logged by the Brooklyn Exchange 'came chiefly from persons with relatives in Queens.' The Brooklyn Exchange makes no comment.

columns.headline: State inspectors' own office system found to need a licence under the Act
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane's office states that the house system of the State inspectors' office in the Borough Hall annex, installed in 1922, has been found to need a licence, and that its two inspectors will examine each other's applications at 10 a.m. today.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Athletics beat the Yankees 6 to 4 at Philadelphia and lead the American League by half a game.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 66. Saturday. Brooklyn has found someone to blame. Us.

lead.headline: Brooklyn's paper traces the Hum to a party line of Queens cousins
lead.deck: Mr. Tully of the Courier signs his name to it: the Greenpoint callers have relatives in Queens and caught it off them; Greenpoint's grandmothers ring in to object
lead.body: Mr. Ambrose Tully, editor of the Brooklyn Courier, has explained Brooklyn's two hundred and twelve night callers. They have relatives in Queens. The Hum, it seems, is caught at Sunday dinner, like a cold or an opinion. Greenpoint has taken this badly. By noon the Courier's switchboard had forty calls from grandmothers who have never been north of Newtown Creek and wished it known. One said she had heard the tone since February and told nobody, it being Queens business. Mr. Tully is not taking calls.

columns.headline: Fusco licenses Teague, Teague licenses Fusco, and the desk takes the credit
columns.body: This morning the State's two licence inspectors, Mr. Fusco and Mr. Teague, licensed each other's office systems seven minutes apart, then found they had licensed the same system twice, it being under the desk they share. The desk is now the most licensed object in Queens.

columns.headline: Athletics pass the Yankees, and Philadelphia turns up the volume
columns.body: Mr. Grove beat the Yankees six to four at Shibe Park and the Athletics are half a game in front. Mr. Huggins says it is May. Philadelphia says it is first place. The Babe went hitless and signed eleven baseballs on his way out.

columns.headline: The Hum's weekly count tunes in at twelve hundred and forty
columns.body: Twelve hundred and forty Queens calls about the night tone this week, up again, and two hundred and twelve from Brooklyn, which says it has none. Dr. Rastin's meter reads forty-one. St. Mary's says a weeknight. He asked which. The rectory is praying on it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: A grey coat was seen at the Arcade again at noon. It bought a Record from the news stand. It did not want the Speaker.

editorial.headline: A letter from the Editor's mother
editorial.body: We print, at her insistence, a letter from Mrs. Agatha Grail of Jamaica, who writes: 'Barnaby, you have written about that woman for six months and not once about your own dinner. Eat something. She is doing more good than you are and she is doing it in heels.' This paper has always believed in a mother's place, which is at home, writing letters to her son that he need not answer. We publish this one to show our readers the depths to which this Lilith has dragged the women of Queens. Even mothers. We have, however, eaten something. It was very good. Miss Penrose recommended the place.

lead.headline: Retired ice horse found on the Steinway route, 11 miles from Bayside
lead.deck: Major left his field about midnight, the company states; made 14 of his former stops before the wagon reached him; returned to Bayside by van at 9 a.m.
lead.body: Major, the grey horse retired on April 20 after 22 years on the Astoria Lake Ice Co.'s Steinway route, was found at Steinway Street and 30th Avenue at 6:10 a.m. yesterday, about 11 miles from the Bayside field to which he was retired, the company's manager, Mr. Gustave Pohl, states. Residents report that he stopped at 14 of his former stops before the wagon, drawn by Duchess, came up behind him at 6:20 a.m. He was returned by van at 9 a.m.

columns.headline: St. Mary's fixes Wednesday night for Dr. Rastin's measurement in the church
columns.body: The rectory of St. Mary's, Long Island City, states that Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia will be admitted to the church at 9 p.m. Wednesday with his meter, 'and will leave at 1 a.m., with or without a reading.' The organ will not be played.

columns.headline: Pastor asks Mr. Crane whether a sanctuary is 'a building within the Act'
columns.body: The Rev. Dr. Elias Hartwell of the Steinway Reformed Church has written to Mr. Hollis Crane asking whether the church's house system, installed in 1909, requires a licence, 'the sanctuary being held by us but not owned by us, in the ordinary sense.' Mr. Crane will reply.

columns.headline: Little America reports 'all well, 55 below' and asks after the Yankees
columns.body: The Navy's station at Bay Shore heard Little America at 10:20 p.m. yesterday, the camp reporting 'all well, 55 below, sun returning in August' and asking 'why the Yankees are second.' The station replied that it did not know.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Major was reported standing at the gate of his Bayside field at 6 p.m., facing west, Mr. Pohl states.

speaker.ear: Mild. High 68. Sunday. Major went to work. Nobody asked him to.

lead.headline: Major won't take retirement lying down, and reconnects the Steinway route
lead.deck: The old ice horse leaves Bayside at midnight, walks eleven miles, and is standing at 30th Avenue for his six o'clock; fourteen kitchens put out carrots before Duchess catches up
lead.body: Somebody in Bayside forgot to shut a gate, or Major remembered how to open one. Either way, at six yesterday morning the old grey was at Steinway Street and 30th Avenue, eleven miles from his field, waiting for his wagon. He did fourteen stops without it. Fourteen kitchens put out carrots and two put out ice cards from habit. When Duchess came up with the wagon at twenty past, she stopped behind him and waited her turn. Mr. Pohl sent a van. Major went home in it like a bishop.

columns.headline: Dr. Hartwell asks Mr. Crane whose name goes on the Lord's line
columns.body: The Steinway Reformed Church wants to know whether its sanctuary, wired in 1909, needs a licence. Dr. Hartwell writes that the church is held by his congregation but not, in the ordinary sense, owned. Mr. Crane must now decide who signs. Dr. Hartwell has a suggestion.

columns.headline: Rastin gets Wednesday night at St. Mary's, and the organ gets the night off
columns.body: Dr. Rastin will be let into St. Mary's at nine on Wednesday with his meter and let out at one, reading or no reading. The organ will be silent. So, the rectory asks, will Dr. Rastin. He says he always is. It is the meter that talks.

columns.headline: Little America picks up the standings, and wants a second opinion
columns.body: Fifty-five below and the sun not back till August, and what Little America wanted to know last night was why the Yankees were second. Bay Shore said it did not know. We do. Philadelphia. Mr. Huggins says it is May. In Little America it is always February.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Major is back in Bayside, standing at the gate, facing Steinway. Mr. Pohl has put a second bolt on it.

lead.headline: State inspectors license each other's office systems at the Borough Hall annex
lead.deck: Mr. Delbert Fusco grants Mr. Amos Teague's application at 10:12 a.m.; Mr. Teague grants Mr. Fusco's at 10:19 a.m.; the two systems found afterward to be one
lead.body: Mr. Delbert Fusco and Mr. Amos Teague, the State's two inspectors under the Listening Act at the Queens Borough Hall annex, licensed each other's office systems on Saturday morning. Mr. Fusco examined and granted Mr. Teague's application at 10:12 a.m., and Mr. Teague granted Mr. Fusco's at 10:19 a.m. Mr. Hollis Crane's office states that the two applications were found afterward to describe the same system, installed in 1922 beneath the desk the inspectors share, which is accordingly licensed twice.

columns.headline: Athletics lead by a game and a half; Yankees lose at Philadelphia and at home
columns.body: The Athletics beat the Yankees 4 to 3 in ten innings at Philadelphia on Saturday, and Washington beat them 5 to 1 at the Stadium yesterday. The Athletics lead the American League by a game and a half. Mr. Ruth had one hit in eight times at bat.

columns.headline: First light bills at 7.5 cents to be read in Astoria and Steinway today
columns.body: Meter readers of Queens Light & Power begin reading the first bills at the domestic rate of 7.5 cents the kilowatt-hour in Astoria and Steinway today, the company states. Alderman John Feeney's petition against the increase will be heard by the Public Service Commission on May 14.

columns.headline: Senate record of March 27 to be kept 'in the vault, not the archive'
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27, containing the word 'resent,' will be kept 'in the vault, not the archive,' at Senator Rufus Keel's request, until the next session. No claimant has come forward.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the twenty-fifth night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 70. Monday. Philadelphia is in first place, and it sounds like it.

lead.headline: Yankees lose the signal at Shibe Park, and the Athletics take the top line
lead.deck: Beaten in ten at Philadelphia and by Washington at home; the Babe gets one hit in eight trips; the Athletics' rooters bring a brass band and a grudge
lead.body: The Yankees went to Philadelphia on Saturday in second place by half a game and came home a game and a half down, the Athletics winning four to three in the tenth, and yesterday at the Stadium Washington beat them five to one for good measure. The Babe had one hit in eight trips. Number 3 is not the trouble, Mr. Huggins says, without saying what is. At Shibe Park the Athletics' rooters brought a brass band and played it every time Mr. Ruth swung. He swung a good deal.

columns.headline: Meter men read the half cent, and Astoria reads the meter men
columns.body: The light company's readers came through Astoria today with their books and their new rate. One was followed three blocks by a woman with a pencil checking his sums. They agreed on everything except the half cent, which she disputes on principle. The Commission sits on the fourteenth.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Twenty-five nights off the air, and our man is off his food
columns.body: We have rung the Radio Division every night at eleven since Tuesday. The night clerk now says 'No, and good night' in one breath. Our man says it is like ringing a sweetheart who has moved. Pin ninety-seven is still in its saucer.

columns.headline: The Senate keeps 'resent' in the vault, and nobody rings to claim it
columns.body: The word taken down in the committee room on March twenty-seventh is to stay in the vault, not the archive, till the next session, at Senator Keel's request. Nobody has come forward to say they said it. Nobody wants to be the one who resents it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The State's desk in the Borough Hall annex is licensed twice. The chair is asking questions.

lead.headline: Sanctuary is 'a building within the Act,' Mr. Crane rules; church to apply
lead.deck: Reply to the Rev. Dr. Hartwell dated May 6; the form to be signed 'by the person in charge of the premises'; Dr. Hartwell to sign 'as tenant' and to preach on the question tonight
lead.body: Mr. Hollis Crane has ruled in a letter to the Rev. Dr. Elias Hartwell of the Steinway Reformed Church that a house of worship is 'a building within the meaning of the Act' and that its house system, installed in 1909, must be licensed by July 1. The form is to be signed 'by the person in charge of the premises.' Dr. Hartwell stated that he will sign it 'as tenant, under protest,' and will preach on it at 10:30 p.m. tonight over WLBQ.

columns.headline: Brooklyn Exchange logs 96 further calls; the Courier's telephone 'engaged'
columns.body: The Brooklyn Exchange logged 96 calls reporting a tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. on Saturday and Sunday nights, chiefly from Greenpoint, its superintendent, Mr. Oswald Pryce, states. The Brooklyn Courier's office telephone was engaged throughout yesterday afternoon.

columns.headline: Mrs. Grieve's members to record their mothers for the capsule on Sunday
columns.body: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve states that the thirteen members who left the Phonautograph Society will record the mothers of members at the Flushing Free Library on Sunday, Mother's Day, for the capsule to be sealed June 15. Record No. 23 has not been returned by Mr. Cyril Abbot.

columns.headline: Valves steady at a dollar the six; eggs at 39 cents the dozen
columns.body: Valves of the common household grade sold steady at a dollar the six at Jamaica and Long Island City yesterday, the Queens Retail Grocers' Association states, and fresh eggs at 39 cents the dozen, up a cent. Long-life valves were quoted at 25 cents each.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states that this newspaper's inquiries regarding WORS 1610 'are logged.'

speaker.ear: Showers. High 63. Tuesday. The State will license the Lord by July.

lead.headline: Albany says the Lord's house needs a licence, and the pastor signs as lodger
lead.deck: Mr. Crane rules a church is a building; Dr. Hartwell will sign 'as tenant, under protest,' and preach on it tonight over WLBQ at half past ten
lead.body: The Listening Act has now asked a church who owns the church. Mr. Crane says the sanctuary of the Steinway Reformed Church, wired since 1909, is a building and must be licensed by July. The form wants the person in charge of the premises. Dr. Hartwell says that is not him, but he will sign as tenant, under protest, and take it up with his landlord tonight over WLBQ at half past ten. We will be listening. So, he hopes, will someone else.

columns.headline: Greenpoint keeps calling, and the Courier's line is always engaged
columns.body: Ninety-six more Greenpoint callers reported the night tone over the weekend. The Brooklyn Courier spent Monday afternoon with its telephone engaged. Brooklyn says the Courier was ringing its Queens relatives. The Courier says the Courier was busy. Both statements are true.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: thirteen mothers will be pressed into service Sunday
columns.body: Darlings, Mrs. Grieve's thirteen will record their mothers for the capsule at Flushing on Sunday. Each mother gets three minutes. One has asked for six and been refused, and one has asked what she is to say and been told 'anything.' She has been rehearsing since.

columns.headline: Valves hold at a dollar the six, and eggs crack a cent higher
columns.body: Household valves held at a dollar the six this week and eggs went up a cent to thirty-nine the dozen. The grocers report the two together, as is the custom. A valve lasts six weeks. An egg lasts breakfast. Shop accordingly.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Hartwell is on the air. If anybody answers, you will read it here first.

lead.headline: WORS 1610 heard at 11:02 p.m. after 27 nights; a sermon on WLBQ ended at 11:01
lead.deck: The Radio Division's shore stations log 14 minutes of figures; the Rev. Dr. Hartwell's last words over WLBQ: 'Is anyone in this house listening?'; the Exchange logs 307 inquiries
lead.body: WORS 1610 was heard at 11:02 p.m. yesterday for the first time since April 10, the Radio Division states, its shore stations logging 14 minutes of figures before the transmission ended at 11:16 p.m. The Rev. Dr. Elias Hartwell's sermon over station WLBQ, 'On the Licensing of a Sanctuary,' had ended at 11:01 p.m. with the words: 'Is anyone in this house listening?' The Exchange logged 307 inquiries. Mr. Harold Pike stated that the Division 'notes the times.'

columns.headline: Dr. Rastin to be admitted to St. Mary's at 9 p.m. tonight with his meter
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia will be admitted to St. Mary's Church, Long Island City, at 9 p.m. tonight with his meter, the rectory states, to measure the tone recorded at 41 cycles on the Holy Saturday record. He will leave at 1 a.m.

columns.headline: Steinway Reformed Church's form received, signed 'as tenant, under protest'
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane's office states that the licence form of the Steinway Reformed Church was received at 9 a.m. yesterday, signed by the Rev. Dr. Elias Hartwell 'as tenant, under protest,' the line for the owner's name left blank. It will be heard on Monday.

columns.headline: Magistrate Haber to give his decision on the two Ostrow records tomorrow
columns.body: Magistrate Leonard Haber will give his decision at 10 a.m. tomorrow on the charge against Mr. Karl Ostrow, tinsmith, whose May Day speech was recorded differently by the Police Department's sound wagon and the United Workers' Committee's machine. Both records remain in the court's keeping.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Rev. Dr. Elias Hartwell states that he 'did not expect a reply on that frequency' and has no further comment.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 72. Wednesday. WORS is back. It picked up when the pastor asked.

lead.headline: Pastor asks if anyone's listening, and WORS rings back in a minute flat
lead.deck: Twenty-seven nights of dead air, then Dr. Hartwell signs off at one past eleven with a question, and at two past the figures come in; the Exchange lights up like Christmas
lead.body: For twenty-seven nights WORS said nothing. Last night at one minute past eleven Dr. Hartwell finished his sermon on WLBQ with a question, 'Is anyone in this house listening?', and at two minutes past, somewhere off the river, WORS came on with its figures and kept on for fourteen minutes, stopping at sixteen past, which is where it stopped last month. The Exchange took three hundred and seven calls. Dr. Hartwell says he did not expect a reply on that frequency. Mr. Pike notes the times.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Right where it wasn't, and the map comes out of the saucer
columns.body: Our office boy put the map back on the wall at half past eleven last night and pin ninety-seven in it, at the river. Mr. Pike's night clerk took our call and said 'Yes' for the first time. He sounded put out.

columns.headline: Rastin gets a pew for the night, and his meter gets religion
columns.body: Dr. Rastin goes into St. Mary's at nine tonight with his meter and comes out at one. The rectory has asked him to remove his hat and keep his voice down. He will do both. The meter has been told nothing. It will do as it likes.

columns.headline: Ostrow's two records stay out of tune till Thursday
columns.body: Magistrate Haber decides tomorrow whether Mr. Ostrow said take the mills or take the mills to the courts. Both records are in one drawer at the court. A clerk says he will not open it till ten, in case they have been talking.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The figures stopped at sixteen past eleven. Four churches have asked Dr. Hartwell to preach on the air. He has not said yes.

lead.headline: Dr. Rastin's meter reads 41 cycles in St. Mary's nave from 9:20 p.m. to 1 a.m.
lead.deck: Strength 'below that at the pavement but steady'; the organ silent and the doors shut; the church's own system recorded the measurement
lead.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia measured a tone of 41 cycles in the nave of St. Mary's Church, Long Island City, from 9:20 p.m. until he left at 1 a.m., the rectory states, at a strength 'below that at the pavement outside, but steady.' The organ was not played and the doors were shut. The church's own house system recorded the measurement, about 220 minutes. Dr. Rastin stated that the reading 'agrees with the Holy Saturday record' and 'with my meter on 31st Street.'

columns.headline: Temperature reaches 81 at 4 p.m.; about 300 persons sleep in Astoria Park
columns.body: The temperature reached 81 at 4 p.m. yesterday and did not fall below 63 overnight, the Weather Bureau states, the first warm night of the year. The Parks Department states that about 300 persons slept in Astoria Park. The Exchange logged 412 complaints of neighbours' sets.

columns.headline: Mr. Pike states the shore stations' log of May 7 is 'complete, figures only'
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states that the shore stations' log of the 14 minutes of WORS 1610 heard on May 7 is 'complete' and contains 'figures only.' The stations will be manned nightly 'from 10:30 p.m.' WORS 1610 was not heard last night.

columns.headline: No decision on the Riverhead seal this week, the Appellate clerk states
columns.body: The clerk of the Appellate Division states that no decision on Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Board of Elections' Riverhead record will be handed down this week. Mr. Gorman has attended each day the court has sat.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Magistrate Haber will give his decision on the Ostrow records at 10 a.m.; Mr. Ostrow states he will 'bring both ears.'

speaker.ear: Warm. High 81. Thursday. Windows open. Queens can hear itself, and its neighbours.

lead.headline: First warm night throws the windows open, and the borough's on a party line
lead.deck: Eighty-one in the afternoon, sixty-three at midnight; every set in Queens turned up and every window up; Astoria Park sleeps three hundred and the Exchange takes four hundred complaints
lead.body: Last night was the first warm night of the year, and Queens did what it does: it opened every window it owns. By nine every set in the borough could be heard by every other, and a man on 21st Street listening to the Philharmonic was also listening to his neighbour's dance band, a baby, a ball game and an argument about a sofa. The Exchange took four hundred and twelve complaints. Three hundred slept in Astoria Park, in their hats. Nobody slept on 21st Street.

columns.headline: Rastin sits up with St. Mary's, and the nave hums along
columns.body: Dr. Rastin spent the night in St. Mary's with his meter and the church's own machine running. Forty-one cycles, from twenty past nine to one, steady, a little softer than the pavement outside. He says it agrees with the Holy Saturday record. He does not say with what else.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I ring my neighbour to turn him down?'
columns.body: Madam, you can, and four hundred and twelve people did last night. The operator connected each of them and could hear both sets down the line, and in some cases her own. She suggests you close your window. She suggests he close his. She suggests summer.

columns.headline: Dolan opens his ground office tomorrow, and asks the ground to call in
columns.body: Mr. Dolan will open his office to hear the ground tomorrow in an empty shop at Steinway Street and Broadway, with a desk, a chair and a man listening. Alderman Feeney says it is a shop with nothing in it. Mr. Dolan says that is the point of a hearing.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pike's shore stations go on at half past ten nightly now. WORS kept them up for nothing.

lead.headline: Charge against Mr. Ostrow dismissed; 'the court cannot prefer one machine'
lead.deck: Magistrate Haber finds both records 'apparently sound, and in disagreement'; both to be kept by the court; the Police Department to examine its sound wagon
lead.body: Magistrate Leonard Haber dismissed the charge of incitement against Mr. Karl Ostrow, tinsmith, of Astoria, in the Long Island City Magistrate's Court at 10:20 a.m. yesterday. The magistrate stated: 'Both records are apparently sound, and they are in disagreement. The court cannot prefer one machine to another, and has no third.' He directed that both records be kept by the court. Captain Thomas Galvin stated that the Department will examine its sound wagon. The United Workers' Committee stated that it will examine nothing.

columns.headline: Second letter from the National Library of Wales delivered to Dr. Strand
columns.body: A second letter from the National Library of Wales, posted April 30, was delivered to Dr. Matthias Strand at Union Seminary yesterday. Dr. Strand stated that it is 'four pages, with a stave,' and that he will not give its contents 'until I have sung it.'

columns.headline: Mr. Dolan to open an 'office to hear the ground' on Steinway Street today
columns.body: Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan will open an 'office to hear the ground' at 10 a.m. today in a vacant shop at Steinway Street and Broadway, his campaign states. The office will contain a desk, a chair and 'a listener, in shifts.' Alderman John Feeney declined to comment.

columns.headline: Florists expect to sell 40,000 carnations in Queens for Sunday
columns.body: The Queens Florists' Association states that its members expect to sell about 40,000 carnations for Mother's Day on Sunday, white at 10 cents and red at 12 cents. The Exchange expects about 3,000 long-distance calls from Queens on Sunday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding, Detective Sergeant Edward Moran states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 78. Friday. Two machines heard one man two ways. The man walked.

lead.headline: Magistrate can't choose between two records, so Ostrow gets off the turntable
lead.deck: Both machines sound, both machines sure, and they disagree by three words; Haber says the court has no third ear and dismisses; Captain Galvin will look at his wagon very hard
lead.body: Mr. Ostrow, tinsmith, went home to his tins yesterday a free man, and the reason is the strangest ruling of the year. Magistrate Haber played the police record and the Committee's record once more, listened to them part company at the mills, and said that both were sound, both disagreed, and the court could not prefer one machine to another and had no third. Case dismissed. Captain Galvin will examine his sound wagon. The Committee will examine nothing, being satisfied. The mills have not been consulted.

columns.headline: Party Line sits out a sixth Friday, and the line still won't ring
columns.body: Six Fridays. At four Party Line was in the parcel window, at five she was asleep in it, and at six she got down and stretched. The lineman's warrant is still outstanding, Sergeant Moran says. The warm end of the board now has to share her with the open window.

columns.headline: Wales sends Strand a note, and he won't let anyone else hear it
columns.body: Wales has written again: four pages and a line of music. Dr. Strand says he will not say what is in it until he has sung it. He has been in a practice room at Union Seminary since three. The porter says it is the same bar over and over.

columns.headline: Mother's Day: forty thousand carnations and three thousand reverse charges
columns.body: The florists of Queens expect to sell forty thousand carnations by Sunday, white at a dime and red at twelve cents. The Exchange expects three thousand long-distance calls, most of them to mothers, many of them asking her to pay. She will. She always has.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Captain Galvin's sound wagon has been towed to the Police Department's garage for examination. It went quietly.

lead.headline: Week's count: 1,410 night calls on the tone in Queens and 340 in Brooklyn
lead.deck: Bushwick and Flatbush report for the first time; Dr. Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles; the Brooklyn Courier states it 'has no knowledge of the figures'
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,410 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 1,240 the week before, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The Brooklyn Exchange logged 340, its superintendent, Mr. Oswald Pryce, states, of which 61 came from Bushwick and 8 from Flatbush, the first from either. Dr. Emil Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles. The Brooklyn Courier states that it 'has no knowledge of the figures.' Queens Light & Power made no statement.

columns.headline: Mr. Dolan's 'office to hear the ground' opens with one listener and 40 callers
columns.body: Mr. Augustin Dolan's 'office to hear the ground' opened at 10 a.m. yesterday at Steinway Street and Broadway with a desk, a chair and Mr. Rudolph Senn, retired stationmaster, listening. About 40 persons called. Mr. Senn's log for the day reads 'traffic, a dray, a bell, nothing else.'

columns.headline: Licences: 318 granted in the week, 757 in all; church listed for Monday
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 318 licences under the Listening Act in the five days to Friday, 757 in all, his office states. Of 6,000 forms delivered on April 9, 2,140 have been returned. The application of the Steinway Reformed Church will be heard at 10 a.m. Monday.

columns.headline: Ice companies report 14 per cent more stops during the warm spell
columns.body: The Astoria Lake, Jamaica Pond and Flushing Bay ice companies report about 14 per cent more stops on Wednesday and Thursday than on the same days last week. Mr. Gustave Pohl states that Duchess has learned the Steinway route 'as far as the dentist's.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Captain Thomas Galvin states that the examination of the sound wagon 'has found nothing wrong with it.'

speaker.ear: Cooler. High 66. Saturday. Call your mother tomorrow. She is already by the telephone.

lead.headline: Dolan's ground office opens for business, and the ground doesn't call
lead.deck: A desk, a chair and Mr. Senn, retired stationmaster, listening in shifts at Steinway and Broadway; forty callers, a dray, a bell; Alderman Feeney walks past twice with Duke
lead.body: Mr. Dolan's office to hear the ground opened yesterday at ten in an empty shop at Steinway Street and Broadway, and it is exactly what he promised: a desk, a chair, and Mr. Rudolph Senn, retired stationmaster, listening. Forty people came in to watch him do it. Mr. Senn's log for the day reads, in full, 'traffic, a dray, a bell, nothing else.' Alderman Feeney walked past twice with Duke. Duke stopped at the door, listened for some time, and would not be moved. Mr. Senn wrote him down.

columns.headline: The Hum's count climbs to fourteen hundred, and Brooklyn's reaches Bushwick
columns.body: Fourteen hundred and ten Queens calls about the night tone this week, and three hundred and forty from Brooklyn, including sixty-one from Bushwick and eight from Flatbush. The Brooklyn Courier says it has no knowledge of the figures. It has now been told them. It still has no knowledge.

columns.headline: Police sound wagon passes its examination, and still won't change its tune
columns.body: Captain Galvin's men have taken the sound wagon apart and found nothing wrong with it. The Committee's machine has not been taken apart, being satisfied with itself. Mr. Ostrow is back at his tins. Both records sit in a drawer at the court, keeping their own counsel.

columns.headline: Duchess gets the route down cold, as far as the dentist's
columns.body: Fourteen per cent more stops for the ice wagons in the warm spell, and Duchess has learned the Steinway route as far as the dentist's, where she still stops. The dentist has started buying ice. Mr. Pohl calls it a new account. Major is said to be sulking in Bayside.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS was not heard tonight by eleven. Dr. Hartwell preaches in Woodside tomorrow, off the air, by choice.

editorial.headline: Nurses paid at last; hospital board blames the moon
editorial.body: The nurses of St. Michael's Hospital, who work twelve hours for the wage of a porter's eight, were paid their arrears in full on Friday after the hospital board's chairman, Mr. Reginald Thorne, delivered to them, in person and in his nightshirt, the cheque. He has explained to us that he was walked in his sleep by a lady in black from his own bedroom to the nurses' home, a distance of a mile, and that she held his hand the whole way and sang. He says she sang well. On the eve of Miss Nightingale's birthday the Speaker honours those who nurse. We do not honour midnight walks. We do note that Mr. Thorne has never before been seen at the nurses' home awake.

lead.headline: Exchange books 2,860 long-distance calls in advance for Mother's Day
lead.deck: Operators to work double shifts from 7 a.m.; calls limited to six minutes from noon 'except where the mother is speaking'; thirteen mothers to be recorded at Flushing
lead.body: The Queens Exchange had booked 2,860 long-distance calls for today by 9 p.m. yesterday, the largest number ever booked in advance, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, 38 of them to Ireland. Operators will work double shifts from 7 a.m. Calls will be limited to six minutes from noon 'except where the mother is speaking.' At the Flushing Free Library the thirteen members who left the Phonautograph Society will record their mothers, three minutes each, for the capsule to be sealed June 15.

columns.headline: Florists report about 37,500 carnations sold by Saturday evening
columns.body: The Queens Florists' Association states that its members had sold about 37,500 carnations by 8 p.m. yesterday, white at 10 cents and red at 12 cents. Several shops in Jamaica sold out of white by 4 p.m. and offered pink 'at the white price.'

columns.headline: Dr. Hartwell to preach at Woodside today; WLBQ not to carry the sermon
columns.body: The Rev. Dr. Elias Hartwell of the Steinway Reformed Church will preach at the Woodside Methodist Church at 11 a.m. today. WLBQ will not carry it, 'at the preacher's request.' WORS 1610 has not been heard since 11:16 p.m. on May 7.

columns.headline: Little America sends 42 Mother's Day messages for relay by wire
columns.body: The Navy's station at Bay Shore states that it received 42 Mother's Day messages from Little America between 9 p.m. and 10:40 p.m. yesterday, for relay by wire to the men's mothers. The camp reported 'all well, 48 below.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Exchange states that bookings for Mother's Day stood at 3,112 at 11 p.m.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 70. Sunday. Mother's Day. Ring her. The operator will know if you don't.

lead.headline: Queens rings its mothers, and the Exchange runs out of switchboard
lead.deck: Three thousand long-distance calls booked, operators on double shifts, six minutes apiece after noon unless Mother is talking, which she will be
lead.body: Today the whole borough telephoned its mother, and the Queens Exchange, with three thousand calls booked to Scranton, Cleveland, Albany and County Cork, put every operator it has on double shifts from seven. After noon each call was limited to six minutes, except where the mother was speaking, which Mr. Arne wrote into the rule because he has one. Our own operator was on the Ohio board all day. She says she heard more mothers than she has had hot dinners. She will ring her own at midnight.

columns.headline: Byrd's men put forty-two calls through to Mother, long distance and then some
columns.body: Little America sent forty-two messages last night for Mother's Day, one from each man, relayed from Bay Shore by wire. Forty-eight below. The Navy says it did not read them. The Navy read them. One said only 'Warm. Fed. Sorry about the window.'

columns.headline: Jamaica's florists run out of white, and paint the town pink
columns.body: Jamaica sold out of white carnations by four yesterday and offered pink at the white price, a dime. White is for a mother gone, red for a mother living. Pink, a florist told us, is for a mother who has not decided.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: thirteen mothers on the record, one for four minutes
columns.body: Darlings, at Flushing this afternoon Mrs. Grieve's thirteen recorded their mothers, three minutes each. The one who asked for six got four, by intrigue. The one who did not know what to say wrote it down. It was a recipe. It will keep till 1978.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Three thousand one hundred and twelve calls booked by last night. Mr. Arne's mother rang him.

lead.headline: Exchange completes 3,604 long-distance calls on Mother's Day, the most in a day
lead.deck: Average call 7 minutes 40 seconds, the six-minute limit 'waived in most cases'; two operators at the Jamaica board relieved; thirteen mothers recorded at Flushing
lead.body: The Queens Exchange completed 3,604 long-distance calls yesterday between 7 a.m. and midnight, the largest number in a day in its history, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The average call lasted 7 minutes 40 seconds, the six-minute limit from noon having been 'waived in most cases, the mother speaking.' Two operators at the Jamaica board were relieved for fatigue. The thirteen former Phonautograph members recorded their mothers at Flushing, 44 minutes in all.

columns.headline: Athletics lead by three games; the Yankees divide two at the Stadium
columns.body: The Athletics beat Cleveland twice and lead the League by three games. The Yankees beat Detroit 6 to 2 on Saturday and lost 4 to 3 yesterday at the Stadium, Mr. Ruth hitting a home run in the ninth with none on. Brooklyn lost at Chicago.

columns.headline: Commission to sit at 10 a.m. tomorrow on the 41 cycles and the light rate
columns.body: The Public Service Commission will give its reserved finding on the two Astoria readings of 41 cycles and hear Alderman John Feeney's petition against Queens Light & Power's rate of 7.5 cents at its sitting at 10 a.m. tomorrow, Commissioner Maurice Lacey's office states.

columns.headline: Steinway Reformed Church's application to be heard at 10 a.m. today
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane will hear the application of the Steinway Reformed Church for a licence under the Listening Act at 10 a.m. today at the Queens Borough Hall, the Rev. Dr. Elias Hartwell having signed as tenant. Members of four congregations have asked to attend.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 has not been heard since 11:16 p.m. on May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Showers. High 64. Monday. Philadelphia is three games up and singing.

lead.headline: Athletics stretch the lead to three, and the Yankees can't find the wavelength
lead.deck: Philadelphia beats Cleveland twice; the Yankees win one and lose one at the Stadium, the Babe homering in the ninth with nobody on and nobody much left in the stands
lead.body: The Athletics took two from Cleveland over the weekend and are three games up, and Mr. Mack has begun to smile in a way that frightens Philadelphia. The Yankees beat Detroit on Saturday and lost yesterday by a run, the Babe hitting one into the bleachers in the ninth with the bases empty and most of the crowd already on the elevated. The Stadium's register gave it fourteen points. Mr. Huggins says it is still May. It will be June shortly. He knows.

columns.headline: Mothers hold the line seven minutes forty, and the limit rings hollow
columns.body: Three thousand six hundred and four calls yesterday, the most in the Exchange's history, and the average call ran seven minutes and forty seconds, the six-minute rule having been waived wherever Mother was speaking. Two Jamaica operators had to be relieved. They went and rang their mothers.

columns.headline: The church draws a full house, and a blank where the landlord goes
columns.body: Mr. Crane heard the Steinway Reformed Church's application this morning with four congregations in the corridor, singing quietly. Dr. Hartwell signed as tenant. Mr. Crane granted the licence and left the owner's line blank. He says the State is not a theologian. The corridor said amen.

columns.headline: Commission tunes in to forty-one tomorrow, and the company won't hum along
columns.body: Tomorrow at ten the Commission rules on the two Astoria readings and hears Alderman Feeney on the half cent, at one sitting. The light company says the rate concerns no tone. Mr. Dolan's man on Steinway Street says he will be listening. He always is.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Grieve's thirteen mothers have been labelled and shelved till June. One has asked to hear herself back. She has been refused.

lead.headline: Public Service Commission sits at 10 a.m. on the Astoria readings and the rate
lead.deck: Commissioner Lacey to give the reserved finding first; Alderman Feeney, Mr. Tisch and Dr. Rastin to appear; the room to be recorded by the Commission's own system 'and no other'
lead.body: The Public Service Commission sits at 10 a.m. today to give its finding on the two Astoria readings of 41 cycles, then to hear Alderman John Feeney's petition to suspend Queens Light & Power's domestic rate of 7.5 cents the kilowatt-hour, Commissioner Maurice Lacey's office states. Alderman Feeney, Mr. Roland Tisch for the company and Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia are to appear. The room will be recorded by the Commission's own system 'and no other,' other machines to be left at the door.

columns.headline: Steinway Reformed Church licensed; the owner's line 'left blank by the State'
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted the Steinway Reformed Church a licence under the Listening Act at 10:40 a.m. yesterday, the Rev. Dr. Elias Hartwell having signed as tenant. Mr. Crane stated that the owner's line 'is left blank by the State, which is not competent to fill it.'

columns.headline: Nine May rent receipts filed with the Municipal Court for the hearing of May 27
columns.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald, counsel for Mr. Oscar Bliss, filed the nine May rent receipts initialled 'S.G.R.' with the clerk of the Municipal Court at Long Island City yesterday. The collector has not been seen at the Vantry Arcade since May 4, the tenants state.

columns.headline: Mr. Dolan's ground office records 212 visitors in its first three days
columns.body: Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan's 'office to hear the ground' at Steinway Street and Broadway recorded 212 visitors in its first three days, his campaign states. The listener's log for Sunday reads in full: 'a church bell, rain, nothing else.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power states that Mr. Tisch 'will bring the company's position, and no machine.'

speaker.ear: Fair. High 68. Tuesday. The Commission has spoken. It said yes and no.

lead.headline: Commission finds the Hum on the level, but not on the light company's line
lead.deck: Both Astoria readings correct, both forty-one, neither the company's, says Mr. Lacey; the half cent goes into a separate account till June the eleventh; Feeney calls it half a victory
lead.body: At ten Commissioner Lacey read his finding. Both Astoria readings were correctly taken. Both found forty-one cycles. The tone is not shown to be carried by the company's conductors. So the Hum is real and belongs to nobody. Then he heard Alderman Feeney on the half cent and reserved again, to June the eleventh, ordering the company to keep the extra half cent in a separate account meanwhile. Mr. Tisch said the company was gratified. He did not say by what.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who's holding my half cent?'
columns.body: Sir, the Commission has told the light company to keep the extra half cent in a separate account till June, so you still pay it, but it is kept apart, like a husband in the spare room. If the Alderman wins, you get it back. If not, it moves in.

columns.headline: Rastin gives the Commission his reading, and it's the same old number
columns.body: Dr. Rastin was asked by the Commission for one thing: his reading at Astoria. He gave it: forty-one. He was asked whether it was the same at St. Mary's and on 31st Street. He said it was. He was not asked anything else, and did not volunteer.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? A week since the sermon, and Hartwell keeps off the air
columns.body: WORS has not been heard since the night Dr. Hartwell asked his question on WLBQ. Four stations have asked him to preach again. He has refused them all. He says he asked once and was answered once, and that is enough conversation for a Reformed minister.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Tisch left the Commission by the side door at five to twelve. Duke was at the front.

lead.headline: Commission finds the Astoria readings correct and the tone 'not the company's'
lead.deck: Commissioner Lacey reads the finding at 10:06 a.m.; the petition on the light rate reserved to June 11; the additional half cent to be held 'in a separate account'
lead.body: The Public Service Commission found yesterday that both readings taken at Astoria were 'correctly taken and agree at 41 cycles,' and that the tone 'is not shown to be carried by the company's conductors,' Commissioner Maurice Lacey reading it at 10:06 a.m. It then heard Alderman John Feeney's petition against the rate and reserved its decision to June 11, directing Queens Light & Power to hold the additional half cent 'in a separate account.' Mr. Roland Tisch stated that the company 'is gratified.'

columns.headline: Dr. Rastin testifies four minutes: 'Forty-one, at Astoria, the same'
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia testified before the Commission for four minutes yesterday. The Commission's record has him at 10:31 a.m.: 'Forty-one. At Astoria, at St. Mary's and on 31st Street, the same.' He was not asked where else, and did not say.

columns.headline: Mrs. Grieve asks Mr. Abbot for record No. 23 a third time
columns.body: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve states that she has written a third time to Mr. Cyril Abbot of the Phonautograph Society for record No. 23, 'to go into the capsule with the mothers.' Mr. Abbot replied yesterday, by messenger, that the record 'is where it was, and is staying.'

columns.headline: Alderman Feeney and Mr. Dolan each state the finding supports him
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney stated that the finding 'leaves Queens paying for a noise nobody owns, until June.' Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan stated that it 'proves an office to hear the ground is needed, since the company cannot.' His listener's log for yesterday reads 'nothing different.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Matthias Strand cabled the National Library of Wales at 6 p.m. yesterday and declines to give the text.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 71. Wednesday. The Hum is official and an orphan.

lead.headline: The man in the grey coat drops in on the court, and won't be served
lead.deck: At twenty to four a man answering the Arcade's description asks the court clerk to see the nine rent receipts, reads them, says 'Correct,' and walks out before anyone thinks of the summons
lead.body: Mr. Raab, process server, has tried Signal Ground Rents' empty post box three times. Yesterday at twenty to four, while Mr. Raab was in the Bronx, a man in a grey coat, about fifty, no hat, walked into the Municipal Court clerk's office at Long Island City and asked to see the nine receipts Mr. Ewald had filed. He read each one. He said 'Correct.' He left. The clerk, who had the summons in a drawer, thought of it as the door shut. Nobody followed him.

columns.headline: Feeney and Dolan both claim the ruling, and split the half cent
columns.body: Alderman Feeney says the ruling leaves Queens paying for a noise nobody owns, till June. Mr. Dolan says it proves the borough needs an office to hear the ground, since the company cannot. Mr. Senn, the office's listener, says he heard the ruling go by. He logged nothing different.

columns.headline: No. 23 is where it was, and Mr. Abbot is staying put on the record
columns.body: Mrs. Grieve has written a third time for record No. 23, to go into the capsule with the thirteen mothers. Mr. Abbot replied by messenger: it is where it was, and it is staying. Mrs. Grieve asked the messenger where he picked up the reply. He has not said.

columns.headline: Strand wires Wales his answer, and won't let us read the cable
columns.body: Dr. Strand cabled the National Library of Wales at six last night, having sung the stave they sent him for two days. He will not give us the text. The telegraph clerk says it was short. We asked how short. He said shorter than the question.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Fire and gas at the Cleveland Clinic this noon; many dead, the Cleveland wire says. No jokes tonight.
